cues.text: Let us now work through some worked questions drawn from the archived continuous assessment.
A few cautions before we begin.
These are paraphrased revision problems from the submitted CA.
The letters you will hear are the archived provisional key, not official marking.
And they are not answers to the unfinished pre-test, so please do not treat them as such.
Let us take the questions in order.
First, CA question two, with the archived letter D.
The scenario: encrypted information is taken, but the encryption keys remain safe.
Why might the reporting risk be lower?
The answer is that the likelihood of readable exposure can be lower.
If an attacker holds only scrambled data and cannot read it, the risk to the people concerned may be reduced.
But be careful.
You must assess the actual statutory threshold.
Encryption is not an automatic exemption from reporting.
The other options are distractors.
Fast remediation, a small record count, and force majeure do not, on their own, independently resolve the duty to report.
So the lesson is this: encryption helps your risk assessment, but it does not by itself switch off the legal duty.
Second, CA question seven, with the archived letter A.
A large Nigerian fintech processes customer financial data and sensitive health data, and claims it has no Data Protection Officer responsibility.
What should you do?
Assess the applicable Nigeria Data Protection Act duties, abbreviated NDPA, together with the designation and registration thresholds.
A large organisation doing large-scale processing of sensitive data warrants serious governance.
It cannot simply rely on an argument based on historical wording to avoid that responsibility.
Third, CA question eight, with the archived letter A.
A university keeps complete fingerprint attendance records indefinitely, even though it only needs to know whether a student was present.
Two principles are implicated here: data minimisation, meaning collect only what you need, and storage limitation, meaning do not keep data longer than needed.
Fingerprints are far more than a presence check requires, and keeping them indefinitely compounds the problem.
Furthermore, if the university also uses these records for secondary analytics, that raises concerns about purpose limitation and about whether there is a lawful basis for the new use.
Fourth, CA question eleven, with the archived letter B.
A bank encrypts its data but maintains disconnected departmental records.
Why could an audit still fail?

Because silos undermine three things: mapping, meaning knowing what data you hold and where; rights handling, meaning responding to individuals' requests consistently; and evidence of consistent controls.
Encryption alone does not give an auditor a coherent picture.
Fifth, CA question seventeen, with the archived letter B, marked as corrected.
A Nigerian health-tech company processes EU-related health records, and faces a conflict between erasure, the right to have data deleted, and statutory medical-record retention requirements.
This is a legal tension.
Resolving it requires analysing whether the relevant rules apply at all, and whether any exceptions are available.
Two further points are worth fixing in your mind.
Hosting data in the European Union is not, by itself, an unlawful transfer.
And there is no blanket NDPA data localisation rule, so Nigerian data need not be kept inside Nigeria simply because of the NDPA.
Finally, do not assume that citizenship alone establishes the scope of the GDPR.
Sixth, CA question twenty-five, with the archived letter B.
A payment company must demonstrate accountability to regulators.
The right approach is to maintain records of processing and evidence of safeguards.
A privacy policy alone is not enough, and neither is a single technical log.
Accountability means being able to show, with documentation, what you do and how you protect the data.
Seventh and last, CA question thirty-seven, with the archived letter A, marked provisional.
A multinational breach may engage the GDPR, Nigerian law, and HIPAA, the United States health privacy law.
The archive suggests an ordered sequence of notification, but no facts justify one authority always coming before another.
The better approach is to assess all the regimes in parallel, looking at their respective thresholds, notification clocks, and the roles the organisation plays under each, and to notify promptly.
For present obligations under the NDPA, use the Nigeria Data Protection Commission, the NDPC.
Notice the common thread across all seven: in each case, assess the actual legal test and the facts, rather than relying on a single control or a convenient assumption.
